#1280. Daily briefing: Are one-person firms the future of biotech?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1003 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Daily briefing: Are one-person firms the future of biotech?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants.
  • Sources indicate that giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) and lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) across Brazil have traces of microplastics circulating in their blood — even if they live more than 60 kilometres away from human infrastructure.
  • Artificial-intelligence giant Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, an upgrade to their AI tool that predicts the molecular effects of ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty.

Sources indicate that giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) and lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) across Brazil have traces of microplastics circulating in their blood — even if they live more than 60 kilometres away from human infrastructure. Researchers found that these animals carry roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood on average — similar to the levels of plastics found in humans — with the highest levels found in those that lived closest to urban areas and waste-management facilities. The findings are an key step to better understand how these particles impact wildlife, states geochemist Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou.

Artificial-intelligence giant Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, an upgrade to their AI tool that predicts the molecular effects of ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences. The tool, announced on 11 November, has already impressed researchers. Its underlying AI model was trained on gene activity and other measurements made in more than 100 million individual cells, across 68 tissues. But the tool can also make predictions when fed data from cell types that it wasn’t trained on, which could help researchers more rapidly identify variants underlying disease, indicates DeepMind scientist Adam Gayoso.

An approach that measures waist circumference and focuses on excess body fat could be a more accurate way to diagnose obesity — and identify people with related health risks — than body mass index (BMI). In an analysis of data from more than 800,000 people, researchers found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The upcoming framework classified an extra 5–9% of people as having obesity, who would have been labelled only as overweight with the BMI-based approach.

Bioengineered bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form for plants could replace up to half of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, slashing the greenhouse-gas emissions associated with these chemicals, researchers suggest. Bacteria can deliver nitrogen to roots more efficiently than synthetic fertilizers, and scientists are engineering them to feed nitrogen to crop plants that don’t have natural microbial partners, such as maize and wheat. Gene-edited biofertilizers have already been used in the United States, but a slew of advances are needed to demonstrate higher levels of nitrogen fixation.

Reference: Nature Biotechnology comment.

In July, artificial-intelligence titan Anthropic acquired a biotechnology firm that developed two promising drug leads with just one full-time human employee and an AI assistant. The mini-firm benefited from the help of several part-time consultants and external research organizations to craft its products — two early-stage antibodies designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy — and many more researchers will be required to take the drugs forward. But the acquisition has sparked discussion about whether one-person, AI-enabled biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future.

Recent findings suggest that with the rise of multidisciplinary science and artificial intelligence, biologists are “poised to at last understand the complexity of life”, writes epigeneticist Edith Heard, chief executive of the Francis Crick Institute, London. But people are what will unlock these discoveries, not technology alone. “Funders, institutions and scientific leaders must embrace new technologies while protecting the conditions in which discovery thrives: curiosity, collaboration and, above all, the freedom and support to follow unexpected observations to see where they lead,” Heard writes.

“Environmental change is altering the conditions in which brains develop and minds are sustained”, states a newly introduced report from a commission convened by Nature Mental Health. For example, heat, air and noise pollution and loss of green space have been linked with depression, anxiety and cognitive decline — with poorer people, children and older people among those most exposed. The Earth–Brain–Health Commission offers a new framework for uniting neuroscience, psychiatry, public health and environmental science around shared challenges and solutions.

Nature Mental Health editorial | 6 min read.

Get the gist in the accompanying policy brief (9 min read).

Reference: Nature Mental Health Earth–Brain–Health Commission report.

The lawless simulated world of blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) — which is just about to release its sixth iteration — offers researchers an intricately crafted testbed for road-safety experiments, says computer scientist Julius Schöning. (BBC | 7 min read).

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03684-x.

Today I’m adding M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything to my reading list. The post-apocalyptic novel was confirmed as the winner of this year’s Booker prize on 9 November — the first “bona fide” science-fiction novel to win the award, indicates Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation.

Let me know what other science-fiction books I should add to the pile, along with your feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing.

With contributions by Flora Graham.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Borussia Dortmundâs brand-newly introduced away kit for the 2025/26 season has sparked fury among supporters, prompting the club to acknowledge the backlash and vow to respond.

The kit, which combines a white base with black sleeves and neon yellow detailing, was worn for the first time in Saturdayâs 2-0 Bundesliga win over Heidenheim.

But instead of excitement, its debut was met with anger in the stands and online. Fans unfurled banners blasting it as âthe cruelest jersey in the leagueâ while chants of âWe want black and yellow jerseysâ rang out before kick-off, a pointed reminder of the clubâs traditional colours.

Sources indicate that across social media, the reaction was no kinder. Many supporters branded the design a betrayal of Dortmundâs historic identity, with critics arguing it looks more like a training top than a shirt fit for the famous Schwarzgelben.

Club bosses have now pledged to listen.

According to recent reports, managing director Carsten Cramer took personal responsibility for the fallout, telling reporters: "The criticism has been received, and we are addressing it. The responsibility lies with me. We won't always be able to please everyone when selecting jerseys.".

Sporting director Sebastian Kehl was more measured, reminding fans that opinions on kit design are always split.

"I think we have different opinions about jerseys every year," he stated. "It will never be the case that a Borussia Dortmund jersey meets with 100 percent approval. Fundamentally, we know which colors represent our city and our club, and that this is reflected in the design of almost all jerseys.".

In a recent development, he added, with a touch of humour: "However, there are also people who want something younger, something fresh, something creative. The new jersey brought BVB three points in Heidenheim. A successful jersey, I'd say. Everything else is a discussion that we as a club consider normal.".

Whether the kit makes another appearance when Dortmund travel to Mainz on September 27 remains to be seen, but if it does, you best believe that Dortmund fans to have something to say about it.
